content: 1. A single trial involving 200 women evaluated the effects of 81 mg of aspirin combined with 200 mg of dipyridamole per day. 2. Another trial, which included 44 women, assessed the combination of 81 mg of aspirin and 200 mg of dipyridamole daily. 3. A separate trial with 91 women investigated the use of 100 mg of aspirin and 300 mg of dipyridamole per day. 4. In a trial involving 76 women, the combination of 125 mg of aspirin and 150–225 mg of dipyridamole daily was studied. 5. A larger trial with 230 women examined the effects of 150 mg of aspirin and 225 mg of dipyridamole per day. 6. Another trial, including 102 women, evaluated the combination of 150 mg of aspirin and 300 mg of dipyridamole daily. 7. A trial involving 127 women assessed the effects of 300 mg of aspirin per week (divided into three doses) combined with 500 mg of vitamin C daily, 400 IU of vitamin E daily, and 1 g of fish oil three times per day. 8. A single trial with 300 women studied the effects of 225 mg of dipyridamole per day. 9. Another trial involving 21 women evaluated 300–400 mg of dipyridamole daily (divided into four doses) combined with 15,000 units of subcutaneous heparin daily (divided into two doses). 10. A trial with 40 women investigated the effects of 400 mg of ozagrel hydrochloride per day. 11. A separate trial involving 160 women assessed the use of 330 mg of triazolopyrimidine daily. Findings on Antiplatelet Agents for Pre-eclampsia Prevention: 12. Across 53 trials involving 37,007 women, placebo was used as the control. In 17 trials with 2,324 women, no antiplatelet agent was used as the control. In five trials involving 789 women, it was unclear whether a placebo was used. 13. The Cochrane review combined aggregate data and individual patient data to estimate the effects of antiplatelet agents. The results from both data types were generally consistent. 14. In cases where the effect estimates diverged significantly or only one type of data was available, this was explicitly noted in the summary. Maternal Outcomes: 15. The effect of antiplatelet agents on maternal death remains unclear due to the low number of events (6/14,339 in the antiplatelet group vs. 3/14,336 in the control group) and very low certainty of evidence. 16. The impact of antiplatelet agents on the risk of cerebrovascular accidents, disseminated intravascular coagulation, liver failure, or renal failure is also unclear, with very low certainty of evidence. 17. None of the included trials reported on maternal intensive care unit (ICU) admissions or other severe maternal morbidity outcomes. 18. The Cochrane review did not report on maternal well-being or satisfaction with the intervention. Subgroup Analyses: 19. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on maternal risk level for pre-eclampsia, gestational age at trial entry, and the dose of antiplatelet agents. 20. Only two priority outcomes—pre-eclampsia and fetal/neonatal death—had subgroup analyses available. 21. Risks of adverse events such as antepartum hemorrhage, postpartum hemorrhage, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage, or other neonatal bleeding were not described by subgroups. Secondary Prevention of Pre-eclampsia: 22. No studies included in the Cochrane review reported on maternal death as an outcome. 23. The effect of antiplatelet agents on the risk of eclampsia among women with gestational hypertension or intrauterine growth restriction is unclear due to very low certainty of evidence. 24. The impact of antiplatelet agents on HELLP syndrome is also unclear due to very low certainty of evidence. 25. None of the included trials reported on maternal ICU admissions or other severe maternal morbidity outcomes. 26. The Cochrane review did not report on Apgar scores, neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage, or other neonatal bleeding among babies born to women using antiplatelet agents for secondary prevention of pre-eclampsia. WHO Recommendations: 27. The WHO recommendations on antiplatelet agents for pre-eclampsia prevention consider the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, maternal risk levels, and timing of intervention initiation. 28. The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent pre-eclampsia is 151 in low-risk women and 39 in high-risk women. 29. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) emphasized the importance of considering baseline maternal risk when issuing recommendations. Cost-effectiveness: 30. Several cost-effectiveness models have demonstrated that aspirin use during pregnancy is a cost-effective intervention for pre-eclampsia prevention. 31. A 2015 decision model analysis of a hypothetical cohort of 4 million women in the USA found that risk-stratified treatment strategies using 81 mg of aspirin were cost-effective. 32. A 2018 decision analysis comparing pre-eclampsia-related costs and effects of four aspirin use strategies found that universal aspirin use was associated with fewer cases of pre-eclampsia and lower overall costs compared to a screen-and-treat approach. 33. In 91% of modeled simulations, universal aspirin use remained the preferred strategy, even when accounting for potential risks such as gastrointestinal bleeding or aspirin-induced asthma. Additional Considerations: 34. Pre-eclampsia increases the risk of adverse outcomes for both mother (e.g., placental abruption, renal failure, liver failure, cerebrovascular accidents, HELLP syndrome, ICU admission) and baby (e.g., fetal/neonatal death, NICU admission). 35. The GDG concluded that these risks make it unlikely that there would be significant variability in how women value the prevention of pre-eclampsia. This detailed breakdown provides a comprehensive understanding of the evidence and recommendations regarding the use of antiplatelet agents for the prevention of pre-eclampsia.
